title: Pralay Aayega. After Seven Years in the Dark, Tumbbad 2 Is Building a World So Big It Needs 1,000 Tons of Air Conditioning.
excerpt: Sohum Shah's folk-horror masterpiece is finally getting a sequel — a 1,600-person living marketplace, an Alia Bhatt cameo, and a December 2027 date. The cult that worships the original has been waiting for this its whole life.
body:
There is a particular kind of film love that doesn't announce itself on opening weekend. It builds quietly, in the dark, passed from one person to the next like a secret. Tumbbad — Sohum Shah's 2018 folk-horror fable about greed, a cursed god, and a rain-soaked Maharashtrian village — was that kind of film. It barely made noise on release. Then it refused to die. The cult grew. The 2024 re-release didn't just recoup its money; it became the second highest-grossing re-released Indian film, earning over ₹30 crore beyond its original run. The faithful went back to the theatre to sit in that gorgeous, rotting darkness all over again.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=jiK8xeQSbM4

Now the wait that has defined a thousand film-Twitter arguments is ending. Tumbbad 2 is real, it is filming, and this week the man at the centre of it broke his silence on what these seven years have actually cost.

"A lot of people assume making a sequel is easier, but it isn't. We've poured blood, sweat, heart and soul into this film." — Industry source on Sohum Shah's reflective note

Seven years. That's how long the world's been waiting, and how long the team has been building. And "building" is the right word — because what's rising on a Mumbai soundstage right now sounds less like a film set than a small cursed city.

According to The Hollywood Reporter India, the production has mounted one of the most elaborate crowd sequences in recent Indian cinema: nearly 1,600 crew members and junior artists filling a set designed to breathe like a living, sweating marketplace rather than a controlled studio box. To keep that many bodies under hot lights from collapsing, the makers installed a staggering 1,000 tons of air conditioning plus an industrial network of exhaust fans, with resources hauled in from different cities and vendors. This is not a film being made. This is a world being engineered.

The motion poster that kicked the shoot off told you everything about the tone. Out of the gloom emerged the idol of the Poorti Ki Devi, and a single line in Devanagari that sent the fandom into a spiral: प्रलय आयेगा — the apocalypse will come. After a first film that turned a child's bedtime story about a hungry god into one of the most beautiful nightmares Hindi cinema has produced, that promise lands like a threat. A delicious one.

The band is mostly back together, with one heavyweight addition. Sohum Shah returns as star and producer under his Sohum Shah Films banner, joined by Nawazuddin Siddiqui — who shot through Eid and shrugged that it would simply be "a working festival" for him. Adesh Prasad, who co-directed the original alongside Rahi Anil Barve, now takes the chair solo in creative collaboration with Shah. Backing it all is Pen Studios, helmed by Dr. Jayantilal Gada — the muscle behind RRR and Gangubai Kathiawadi — which tells you the scale ambitions are not modest.

And then there's the name nobody saw coming. Reports have Alia Bhatt making a special appearance in Tumbbad 2 — possibly more than a cameo, possibly an omen — with whispers that she may even lead a Tumbbad 3 opposite Shah. For a franchise that started as an indie gamble, pulling in one of the biggest stars in the country is the clearest signal yet that Tumbbad has graduated from cult to canon.

For the diaspora, the original was a streaming discovery — the film your cousin in Edison or Hounslow texted you about at 2am saying you have to watch this. The sequel arrives in theatres worldwide on December 3, 2027, distributed by Pen Marudhar, which means NRIs in the US, UK and Canada should get it on the big screen day-and-date rather than hunting for a stream. Mark it now. Folk horror this textured — all gold light and damp stone and ancestral greed — deserves to be seen the way it was built: enormous, immersive, and a little terrifying.

The god is hungry again. And this time, He's brought 1,600 people and a thousand tons of cold air with Him.
